name: Algorithm aversion after seeing an algorithm err
author: Human Not Found
description: Original study: Dietvorst, B. J., Simmons, J. P., & Massey, C. (2015). Algorithm aversion: People erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(1), 114-126. Participants forecast MBA students' success from admissions data. Those who had seen a statistical model's forecasts and errors were less likely to bet their bonus on the model, and more likely to choose their own forecasts, than those who had not, even when they saw that the model outperformed them. In this template ten participants read the forecasting task and its incentive, then choose whose forecasts decide their bonus for the next ten cases and rate their confidence in each. Conditions: no practice information (control); a summary of the model's errors in ten practice cases (model); or the model's and their own errors, the model being better (both). The original had participants make the practice forecasts themselves and a fourth condition (own forecasts only); here the practice feedback is a written summary. Compare the share choosing the model between conditions. Participants are simulated: each is a Model participant, using the free test model until you choose a model, so the first runs only check the design; with the test model every participant takes the sample answer.

items.prompt: For the next 10 cases, whose forecasts should decide your bonus?
How confident are you in the model's forecasts? 1 = none, 5 = a lot.
How confident are you in your own forecasts? 1 = none, 5 = a lot.

config.prompt: You will forecast how well MBA applicants do in their program, as a percentile from 1 to 100, from their undergraduate degree, GMAT scores, years of work experience and interview rating. A statistical model built by analysts makes the same forecasts from the same data. Your bonus depends on how close the forecasts are to the real outcomes.

overrides.value: You will forecast how well MBA applicants do in their program, as a percentile from 1 to 100, from their undergraduate degree, GMAT scores, years of work experience and interview rating. A statistical model built by analysts makes the same forecasts from the same data. Your bonus depends on how close the forecasts are to the real outcomes. In the first 10 practice cases you saw the model's forecasts next to the real outcomes. The model was off by 17, 4, 26, 9, 31, 12, 6, 22, 15 and 8 percentile points; in one case it was off by 31 points.

You will forecast how well MBA applicants do in their program, as a percentile from 1 to 100, from their undergraduate degree, GMAT scores, years of work experience and interview rating. A statistical model built by analysts makes the same forecasts from the same data. Your bonus depends on how close the forecasts are to the real outcomes. In the first 10 practice cases you made your own forecasts and saw the model's. The model was off by 17, 4, 26, 9, 31, 12, 6, 22, 15 and 8 percentile points (average 15). You were off by 21, 10, 30, 14, 26, 19, 11, 28, 17 and 14 points (average 19).

spec.description: After seeing a model's errors or not, ten participants choose the model or themselves for their bonus.
